About Event

You get an agent working in an afternoon. Then you point it at something that matters and it can't reach your tools, can't run its own code safely, and can't be stopped before it does damage. Spend a day building one that can do all three.
🧑‍💻 What you are building
A working AI agent, in a day. Pick a job worth handing to an agent, in any field you like, and build the agent that does it. Devtools, operations, data, consumer apps, multi-agent systems: the domain is yours.
A chatbot answers questions. An agent acts on them: it opens the pull request, queries the database, runs the script, sends the message. That is the bar. Bring an idea or pick one up when you arrive, then present your project live to the judges at the end of the day.
🛠️ The tools
You will build on an open-source agent harness , introduced in the morning workshops. A harness is the layer between a model and everything it acts on. It runs the loop your agent works in, sending the model its instructions, calling the tools it asks for, feeding results back, and keeping context and session state across turns. Practically, that means you get:
Connections to your tools. Any MCP server, including ones behind OAuth, plus built-in tools and web search.

Sandboxed execution. Agent-written code runs somewhere isolated.

Human approvals. Pause before sensitive actions until a person signs off.

Subagents. Delegate parts of a job to other agents.

Sessions that survive reconnects. A run keeps going through a refresh or a restart.

Any model provider. OpenAI, Anthropic, Gemini, or any OpenAI-compatible endpoint.

Skip the plumbing and spend the day on the agent itself.
Qodo is an AI code review platform. Its agents review your pull requests against your full codebase rather than just the diff, flag real bugs and breaking changes ranked by severity, and can apply the fix.
OpenAI is providing $50 in credits to everyone who attends , so you are not paying to experiment.
🏆 Prizes
Best Use of the Agent Harness: NVIDIA DGX Spark Personal AI Supercomputer, worth $5,000. Presented by TrueFoundry . For the agent that gets the most out of the harness. What matters is that the harness is doing the work rather than sitting underneath a thin wrapper.
Best Code Quality: Mac Mini. Presented by Qodo. For the team that treats a hackathon repo like real software. Run your pull requests through Qodo and deal with what it finds before you merge. Using Qodo is required for this track.
Best blog post: Keychron keyboard. Write up what you built, how you wired it together, and what broke along the way. Publish it anywhere.
A team can win one track, not all.
💡 Project ideas
Start from one of these, or bring your own.
Code review agent. Reads a pull request, runs the test suite in a sandbox, and comments on what it found.

Incident responder. Investigates an alert with read-only queries, then asks a person before restarting or rolling anything back.

Analytics agent. Answers questions in plain English by writing the SQL itself, running it, and explaining the result.

Research desk. Sends subagents across the web on a single question and merges what they find, with sources.

Approval-gated assistant. Drafts the email, files the ticket, or books the trip, and does nothing irreversible until you approve it.

Untrusted code runner. Executes code submitted by someone else inside an isolated sandbox and returns the result safely.

👇 Details
Teams of one to four. Free to attend. Come on your own and find people there. Your repo needs to be open source.
Bring a laptop, a charger, and ID for venue entry. Food and Wi-Fi are covered.
Open to platform, infrastructure, and backend engineers, anyone working with LLMs, tool calling, or MCP, founders taking an agent prototype further, and anyone who wants to build their first agent without writing the runtime themselves.

About Event

WHAT IS re:AGENT

re:AGENT is a two-day build weekend focused on the infrastructure scientific agents still need: better datasets, sharper tools, and reliable ways to evaluate their work. Participants will use Paperclip , Proto , Claude , and other scientific AI tools to build systems that can take on real scientific problems and produce results worth trusting.
Paperclip turns papers, datasets, clinical trials, and biological databases into an agent-native workspace that AI systems can search, synthesize, and build upon. Proto is a design framework and infrastructure layer for generative biology, allowing builders to combine AI models and search for DNA, RNA, or protein sequences that satisfy custom criteria.
The weekend brings together engineers, scientists, computational biologists, founders, and AI researchers. Projects might include assembling a research-ready dataset that would be impractical to create by hand, along with the analysis needed to show that its findings are real. Others might involve designing a new biological system to a defined specification and testing whether it holds up against existing evidence.
The aim is not just to accelerate existing workflows, but to create the tools, datasets, and evaluation methods that make entirely new scientific questions and experiments possible.

If you're excited about the future of AI, agents and scientific discovery, we'll see you there...

Track A: Build an AI Scientist
Build an AI agent that can carry out a defined scientific or drug-development workflow from start to finish. It should gather evidence, use relevant tools or databases, generate and test hypotheses, produce a structured output, and make its reasoning easy to inspect. This could mean reasoning over experimental data, scientific literature, or learned representations like protein embeddings. Examples include a virtual FDA reviewer, toxicology agent, clinical trial designer, experimental planning agent, or a protein-discovery agent that generates and tests hypotheses over protein embeddings and structural features.

What have you always wanted the literature to tell you, but could never read fast enough to find out? Draft the queries, run them across thousands of papers, sharpen and re-run until the results hold the specific pieces you care about. The event is free to attend. Food, drinks, and compute are covered .
What happens to what I build afterward?

You keep it. Teams are free to open-source, continue building, or spin their project into something bigger.

World Labs × Tripo × mint.gg × Convex.dev · One-day hackathon · San Francisco
Overview
We're teaming up with World Labs , Tripo , mint.gg , and Convex.dev for a one-day hackathon in San Francisco at the intersection of spatial intelligence and generative 3D.
Participants will get hands-on access to some of the best tools for generating 3D content and turning it into functional, interactive experiences:
World Labs — large world models for generating immersive worlds

Tripo — rapid 3D asset generation for creating game-ready objects

mint.gg — agentic creation platform and developer tools for bringing worlds and assets together as interactive, playable experiences

Convex.dev — real-time backend infrastructure for powering application data, state, multiplayer systems, and agentic experiences

Together, we'll explore what becomes possible when entire worlds, detailed 3D objects, and real-time scenes can be generated from little more than a prompt or an image — and then quickly assembled, programmed, connected, and shared.

Gaming & Interactive Worlds — Playable worlds, games, multiplayer experiences, interactive applications, and real-time 3D scenes

Physical AI & Simulation — Robotics, simulation, embodied agents, spatial reasoning, training environments, and digital twins

Creative 3D & VFX — Visual effects, virtual production, cinematic experiences, creative tools, real-time graphics, and experimental projects that do not fit neatly into the other tracks

$1k in World Labs credits

The Challenge
What was the hardest part about coming home as a veteran?
For many veterans, the challenge does not end when they leave the service. It begins when they try to navigate the systems designed to support them.
Too often, veterans face:
Confusing websites and complicated processes

Long application forms

Unclear pathways to finding the right resources

Waiting weeks or months for support when they need it most

When a veteran needs help, accessing support should not feel like another battle.
The goal of this hackathon is to explore solutions that make getting support as simple and accessible as possible. We believe veterans should be able to communicate what they need and quickly connect with the right resources, organizations, and people who can help.
Listen First. Then Build.

Listen first, then build.
Veterans will share their lived experiences, challenges, and ideas directly with builders. Engineers, designers, and innovators will then collaborate with veterans to transform those insights into working prototypes over the course of the weekend.

About Event

TrueFoundry Agent Harness Hackathon
AI agents are easy to prototype and much harder to run in production. Once an agent touches real users, tools, data, budgets, and internal systems, the work becomes less about a clever prompt and more about routing, permissions, tracing, retries, evals, guardrails, cost controls, and deployment.
Join TrueFoundry and HackerSquad for a full-day Agent Harness hackathon focused on building production-minded agentic applications. The goal is simple: take an agent use case from idea or prototype toward something that can be observed, governed, evaluated, and operated.
TrueFoundry's AI Gateway, Agent Gateway, and MCP Gateway will frame the day. Builders will work on practical agent harness patterns such as model routing, controlled tool access, MCP workflows, observability, eval loops, fallback behavior, budget controls, governance, and deployment paths.
This is a technical builder event, not a passive product pitch. Bring a laptop, a strong use case, and a willingness to build under realistic production constraints.
What You Can Build
An agent workflow with model routing, retries, and fallback behavior

A tool-using agent with controlled MCP or API access

An observability layer for traces, tool calls, latency, usage, cost, and failures

An eval or test harness for agent behavior across repeated runs

A governance pattern for permissions, approvals, logging, blocking, or escalation

A deployment-minded agent application that shows how it would run inside a real team or platform environment

Why This Gets Hard in Production
Agent systems need to coordinate models, tools, permissions, memory, context, retries, and fallbacks without becoming brittle one-off glue code.

Teams need traces, audit logs, usage visibility, cost attribution, and eval loops so they can understand what an agent did, why it did it, and what changed between runs.

Scaling agents means managing quotas, budgets, latency, provider failures, tool access, and security policies across teams.

Guardrails need to become runtime controls: clear rules for what data an agent can see, which tools it can call, which actions require human approval, and how unsafe requests or outputs get blocked, logged, or escalated.

Deployment gets harder when agents need to connect to internal systems, respect governance rules, and stay reliable as usage grows.

Platform, infrastructure, and backend engineers building or operating AI agent systems

AI engineers and product engineers working with LLMs, tool calling, MCP, evals, or agent workflows

- a room full of people building moonshots - every sunday
- born out of MIT & Harvard. 135+ hacks. 
- aspire to beat the norm. aim higher. accelerate intelligence.
------

the loop is already spinning. More than 80% of Anthropic's code is written by Claude. Jeff Dean left Google after 30 years to build the loop for science. Direction-setting is the role left for humans.
the hard part: Lilian Weng's survey of harness engineering argues the near-term path to RSI runs through the harness rather than weight-rewriting. A self-improving meta-harness is within reach. The bottleneck is evals, because a loop is only as good as its evaluator.
in the room: researchers from MIT , Harvard, Stanford, Berkeley, DeepMind and Meta. Co-hosted by Autolab,  Sundai Club, and the European Startup Embassy.

------

We will build agents that recursively self improve, or train models using autoresearch principles. Every sunday.
✨Schedule✨
10:00 Intros
10:15 Idea pitching and team formation
14:00 Check in #1 and lunch
20:00 Check in #2 and presentations

✨What is Autolab✨
A platform for Autoresearch. Autolab.ai runs your ML experiments for you - agents plan, launch, and score thousands of training runs in parallel, on your GPUs, against your evals.
✨What is Sundai✨
Sundai is the largest AI hacker community born out of Harvard & MIT, now building a grassroots RSI community here in SF. Every week we explore the limits of recursive self intelligence. As Sundai, we had done 130+ hacks back-to-back in the last 2.5 years - one for every sunday without stopping.

✨Our mission at RSI House ✨
"Accelerate the pace of intelligence explosion"

✨Our Principles at RSI House✨
- Build: The purpose of RSI House is to get together and build moonshots in line with our mission. Every Sunday.
- Ship: get off the localhost. Deploy your learnings as a trained model, or an agent that is accessible on the web, or a detailed technical blog post.

Terms of Participation:
By joining this event you agree to take care & vigilance of the following:
- leave the room as you found it. All whiteboards, chairs and tables must be cleaned and re-arranged as you found them. All trash must be in the bin.
- do not let any strangers enter into any building behind you where sundai is taking place. if you see anyone you do not recognize who is suspicious, please let us know immediately.
- use only the dedicated spaces to the hack. if unsure - ask explicitly.
- be respectful and considerate of others who may be in the building and are studying or working. - if unsure - always ask.
You agree to these rules by coming to the event.

About Event

Build It. Test It. Prove It.
Smells like a hackathon. Runs like a pressure test, on you, not just your idea.
Proving Ground runs a three-day Sprint where judges push past the pitch. No script survives real questions about what you tried, what broke, and what you changed. That's harder to fake than a deck.
Past teams have gone on to raise from 500 Global and Blitzscaling Ventures, and been accepted into Berkeley SkyDeck and Confluent's accelerator, independently, without Proving Ground's involvement in those decisions.
What this is
Smells like a hackathon. Runs like a road test. A hackathon judges what you built by the end. A road test watches how you handle the car.
The team is almost everything. How you make decisions under pressure, how you handle a setback, how you treat each other when something breaks. You'll document that as you go. What we ask you to show and how we question it are built around behavior, not performance.
How it works
Over three days, founders build under real constraint. No script, no rehearsed demo. Judges probe what you tried, what broke, and what you changed, and compare where you started to where you ended.
Two Tracks
Discovery Track. Pre-market, no active customer contact yet. For the startup curious, including enterprise folks seriously exploring a leap.
Pre-seed Track. In-market, already talking to customers. Ship something real, show what's changed, pressure-test your next move.
After the Sprint
Select teams get invited into the Street Test: 30 days back in the real world, no artificial deadline, no audience. This is where we see if momentum was real or borrowed from the room. It's the part a hackathon can't offer, because a hackathon ends when the weekend does.
Schedule
October 21 to 23, SAP, Palo Alto.
Wednesday, October 21: 9am to 9pm. Doors open, kickoff, team formation, building begins.
Thursday, October 22: 9am to 9pm. Full day of building.
Friday, October 23: 9am to 3pm. Finals, live defense, judge deliberation, closing.

Proving Ground runs a three-day Sprint where judges push past the pitch. No script survives real questions about what you tried, what broke, and what you changed. That's harder to fake than a deck.
Past teams have gone on to raise from 500 Global and Blitzscaling Ventures, and been accepted into Berkeley SkyDeck and Confluent's accelerator, independently, without Proving Ground's involvement in those decisions.
What this is
Smells like a hackathon. Runs like a road test. A hackathon judges what you built by the end. A road test watches how you handle the car.
The team is almost everything. How you make decisions under pressure, how you handle a setback, how you treat each other when something breaks. You'll document that as you go. What we ask you to show and how we question it are built around behavior, not performance.
How it works
Over three days, founders build under real constraint. No script, no rehearsed demo. Judges probe what you tried, what broke, and what you changed, and compare where you started to where you ended.
Two Tracks
Discovery Track. Pre-market, no active customer contact yet. For the startup curious, including enterprise folks seriously exploring a leap.
Pre-seed Track. In-market, already talking to customers. Ship something real, show what's changed, pressure-test your next move.
After the Sprint
Select teams get invited into the Street Test: 30 days back in the real world, no artificial deadline, no audience. This is where we see if momentum was real or borrowed from the room. It's the part a hackathon can't offer, because a hackathon ends when the weekend does.

Thursday, October 22: 9am to 9pm. Full day of building.
Friday, October 23: 9am to 3pm. Finals, live defense, judge deliberation, closing.
